descriptionEn: 6-minute test to estimate VO2max (half-Cooper test). Distance covered x 10 = approximate vVO2max. Simple and reliable protocol.

mainSetStructure.description: Test 6 minutes : courir la plus grande distance possible
mainSetStructure.descriptionEn: 6-minute test: run the greatest distance possible

mainSetTemplate.description: Test 6 minutes : courir la plus grande distance possible
mainSetTemplate.descriptionEn: 6-minute test: run the greatest distance possible

coachingTipsEn: Start fast but not sprinting
Maintain constant effort for 6 minutes
Note the distance to the nearest meter
vVO2max (km/h) = distance (m) / 100
commonMistakesEn: Starting too fast and collapsing
Not warming up enough
Running the test on unmeasured terrain

descriptionEn: Test to determine Critical Velocity (CV). Based on two time trials (1200m and 3600m) to calculate CV. Billat protocol.
coachingTipsEn: CV = (D2-D1) / (T2-T1) with D in meters and T in seconds
The 1200m must be run all-out
The 3600m requires good pace management
CV corresponds roughly to 10K-half marathon pace
commonMistakesEn: Not being rested enough for this test
Recovery too short between the two time trials
Poor pacing on the 3600m

descriptionEn: 5K time trial to evaluate current fitness and predict performance over other distances. Classic benchmark.
coachingTipsEn: Manage your pace: the first km should not be the fastest
Aim for even splits
This time allows estimation of VO2max, threshold and marathon paces
Ideally on track or certified course
commonMistakesEn: Starting too fast
Not knowing your target pace
Running the test fatigued

descriptionEn: Field VO2max test with 20m shuttles (VAMEVAL or Luc Leger protocol). Progressive until exhaustion.

mainSetStructure.description: Test navettes 20m progressif (bip sonore) jusqu'à l'arrêt
mainSetStructure.descriptionEn: Progressive 20m shuttle test (audio beep) until failure

mainSetTemplate.description: Test navettes 20m progressif (bip sonore) jusqu'à l'arrêt
mainSetTemplate.descriptionEn: Progressive 20m shuttle test (audio beep) until failure

coachingTipsEn: Need audio track or app for the test
Starting speed: 8 km/h, +0.5 km/h per stage
vVO2max = last completed stage
Scientifically validated test (Leger & Lambert, 1982)
commonMistakesEn: Not having the correct audio file
Distance between cones poorly measured
Stopping before actual exhaustion

descriptionEn: 12-minute endurance test created by Dr. Kenneth Cooper in 1968. Run the greatest distance possible in 12 minutes. Formula: VO2max = (distance in meters - 504.9) / 44.73. Correlation of 0.90 with laboratory-measured VO2max.

mainSetStructure.description: Test 12 minutes : courez la plus grande distance possible à effort soutenu
mainSetStructure.descriptionEn: 12-minute test: run the greatest distance possible at sustained effort

mainSetTemplate.description: Test 12 minutes : courez la plus grande distance possible à effort soutenu
mainSetTemplate.descriptionEn: 12-minute test: run the greatest distance possible at sustained effort

coachingTipsEn: Pace yourself: start at a pace you can hold for 12 minutes, not a sprint
The ideal pace is between your 3000m and 5000m pace
Record total distance to the nearest meter for VO2max calculation
commonMistakesEn: Starting with a sprint and blowing up after 3-4 minutes
Not warming up sufficiently before a maximal effort
Performing the test in hot or windy conditions, skewing results

descriptionEn: Progressive test to determine anaerobic threshold via heart rate deflection. Speed increases by 0.5 km/h every 2 minutes. The deflection point (HRDP) indicates anaerobic threshold. Francesco Conconi protocol (1982).

mainSetStructure.description: Course progressive : démarrer à 8-9 km/h, augmenter de 0.5 km/h toutes les 200m (ou 2 min). Noter FC à chaque palier. Continuer jusqu'à épuisement.
mainSetStructure.descriptionEn: Progressive run: start at 8-9 km/h, increase by 0.5 km/h every 200m (or 2 min). Record HR at each stage. Continue until exhaustion.

mainSetTemplate.description: Course progressive : démarrer à 8-9 km/h, augmenter de 0.5 km/h toutes les 200m (ou 2 min). Noter FC à chaque palier. Continuer jusqu'à épuisement.
mainSetTemplate.descriptionEn: Progressive run: start at 8-9 km/h, increase by 0.5 km/h every 200m (or 2 min). Record HR at each stage. Continue until exhaustion.

coachingTipsEn: An accurate heart rate monitor is essential for this test
The deflection point is where HR stops increasing linearly with speed
Perform the test on a track for precise speed control
commonMistakesEn: Increasing speed irregularly between stages
Not wearing a reliable heart rate monitor
Performing the test while fatigued or dehydrated

descriptionEn: Workout of 10x800m created by Bart Yasso to predict marathon time. The time of each 800m in minutes:seconds predicts marathon time in hours:minutes. E.g., 3:30 per 800m = 3h30 marathon. Recovery equals effort time.

steps.description: 800m à allure cible (temps en min:sec = temps marathon en h:min)
steps.descriptionEn: 800m at target pace (time in min:sec = marathon time in h:min)

between.descriptionEn: 4min easy jog (same duration as the effort)

mainSetTemplate.description: 10x800m à allure cible (temps en min:sec = temps marathon en h:min)
mainSetTemplate.descriptionEn: 10x800m at target pace (time in min:sec = marathon time in h:min)
mainSetTemplate.recoveryEn: 4min easy jog (same duration as the effort)

coachingTipsEn: Build progressively: start with 4x800m and add one rep per week
Recovery must last exactly the same time as the 800m effort
This isn't a precise scientific test but an excellent fitness benchmark
commonMistakesEn: Trying to do all 10 reps from the first session
Running the first 800m reps too fast compared to the last ones
Shortening recovery, which skews the prediction

descriptionEn: Monthly aerobic tracking test by Dr. Phil Maffetone. Run 5 km at MAF heart rate (180 - age, adjusted). Measure time per kilometer: improving times reflect aerobic progress.

warmupStructure.description: Échauffement progressif : marche puis accélération très graduelle sur 12-15 min jusqu'à atteindre la FC MAF
warmupStructure.descriptionEn: Progressive warmup: walk then very gradual acceleration over 12-15 min to reach MAF HR

mainSetStructure.description: 5 km à FC MAF constante (180 - âge). Notez le temps de chaque kilomètre.
mainSetStructure.descriptionEn: 5 km at constant MAF HR (180 - age). Record time for each kilometer.

cooldownStructure.description: Décroissance progressive de l'allure sur 10-15 min

warmupTemplate.description: Échauffement progressif : marche puis accélération très graduelle sur 12-15 min jusqu'à atteindre la FC MAF
warmupTemplate.descriptionEn: Progressive warmup: walk then very gradual acceleration over 12-15 min to reach MAF HR

mainSetTemplate.description: 5 km à FC MAF constante (180 - âge). Notez le temps de chaque kilomètre.
mainSetTemplate.descriptionEn: 5 km at constant MAF HR (180 - age). Record time for each kilometer.

cooldownTemplate.description: Décroissance progressive de l'allure sur 10-15 min

coachingTipsEn: MAF HR must stay constant: if it rises, slow down immediately
The first kilometer is normally the fastest and the last the slowest, this is normal
Repeat this test monthly under the same conditions to track aerobic progress
commonMistakesEn: Not strictly following MAF HR and running too fast
Comparing tests done under different conditions (heat, wind, terrain)
Getting discouraged if initial paces are very slow, that's the normal starting point

descriptionEn: Maximal 3-minute test on track to determine critical speed (CS) and anaerobic reserve (D') in a single effort. The pace of the last 30 seconds corresponds to critical speed.

mainSetStructure.description: 3 minutes d'effort maximal soutenu sur piste. Notez la distance totale et l'allure des 30 dernières secondes
mainSetStructure.descriptionEn: 3 minutes of sustained maximal effort on track. Record total distance and pace of the last 30 seconds

mainSetTemplate.description: 3 minutes d'effort maximal soutenu sur piste. Notez la distance totale et l'allure des 30 dernières secondes
mainSetTemplate.descriptionEn: 3 minutes of sustained maximal effort on track. Record total distance and pace of the last 30 seconds

coachingTipsEn: Start fast from the beginning, the goal is to deplete the anaerobic reserve (D') within the first 150 seconds
Critical speed (CS) = average pace of the last 30 seconds
D' = total distance − (CS in m/s × 180 seconds)
Use GPS or track markers for precise measurement
commonMistakesEn: Pacing the effort like a 1,000m instead of going all-out
Not maintaining maximal effort for the full 3 minutes
Forgetting to record the pace of the last 30 seconds separately

descriptionEn: Incremental step test with 4-5 minute stages on track with progressive speed increases. Identifies both lactate thresholds (LT1 and LT2) and precisely defines all training zones.

mainSetStructure.description: Paliers de 4-5min à vitesse croissante (+0,5 km/h par palier). Départ à ~60% VMA. À chaque fin de palier : noter FC, RPE, lactate si disponible. Continuer jusqu'à épuisement
mainSetStructure.descriptionEn: 4-5min stages at increasing speed (+0.5 km/h per stage). Start at ~60% vVO2max. At end of each stage: record HR, RPE, lactate if available. Continue until exhaustion

mainSetTemplate.description: Paliers de 4-5min à vitesse croissante (+0,5 km/h par palier). Départ à ~60% VMA. À chaque fin de palier : noter FC, RPE, lactate si disponible. Continuer jusqu'à épuisement
mainSetTemplate.descriptionEn: 4-5min stages at increasing speed (+0.5 km/h per stage). Start at ~60% vVO2max. At end of each stage: record HR, RPE, lactate if available. Continue until exhaustion

coachingTipsEn: LT1 (aerobic threshold) ≈ stage where HR increases beyond linear trend (~2 mmol/L)
LT2 (anaerobic threshold) ≈ stage where effort becomes very hard to maintain (~4 mmol/L)
Even without a lactate meter, the HR + RPE combination per stage allows threshold estimation
Perform this test at the beginning of a cycle to calibrate your training zones
commonMistakesEn: Increasing speed too quickly between stages
Not respecting the duration of each stage (full 4-5 minutes)
Forgetting to record data at the end of each stage

descriptionEn: Very easy bike spin in Z1-Z2 to flush the legs, promote venous return and aid recovery without adding fatigue.

mainSetStructure.description: Pédalage souple en Z1, cadence 90-100 rpm
mainSetStructure.descriptionEn: Easy spin in Z1, cadence 90-100 rpm

mainSetTemplate.description: Pédalage souple en Z1, cadence 90-100 rpm
mainSetTemplate.descriptionEn: Easy spin in Z1, cadence 90-100 rpm

coachingTipsEn: Small gear, high cadence, zero leg pressure
Breathe through your nose to stay minimal
Flat roads, no surges
commonMistakesEn: Pushing too hard on any incline
Drifting into Z3 without noticing

descriptionEn: Continuous aerobic ride in Z2. Builds the aerobic base, pedalling economy and fat oxidation capacity. Natural cadence 85-95 rpm.

mainSetStructure.description: Endurance continue en Z2, cadence 85-95 rpm

mainSetTemplate.description: Endurance continue en Z2, cadence 85-95 rpm

Steady cadence, steady effort, you can hold a conversation
Hydrate from 45 min, fuel after 90 min
commonMistakesEn: Starting too fast and accumulating useless fatigue
Neglecting cadence and mashing in big gears

descriptionEn: Upper-tempo / lower-threshold session. Two 15-minute blocks at 88-94 % FTP, 8 minutes recovery between. Builds sustainable aerobic power.

warmupStructure.descriptionEn: Progressive warm-up + 3×1' in Z3 to activate

warmupTemplate.description: Échauffement progressif + 3×1' en Z3 pour activer
warmupTemplate.descriptionEn: Progressive warm-up + 3×1' in Z3 to activate

mainSetTemplate.description: 2×15' en sweet-spot (88-94 % FTP, Z3 haut / Z4 bas), récup 8' entre en Z1

coachingTipsEn: Aim for "comfortably hard", not full Z4
Cadence 85-95 rpm, keep breathing controlled
If the second block falls apart, lower the power rather than abandoning
commonMistakesEn: Going too hard on the first block
Confusing sweet spot with threshold, stay below FTP

descriptionEn: Threshold intervals. Four 8-minute blocks at 95-102 % FTP, 4 minutes recovery between. A staple for lifting the lactate threshold.

mainSetTemplate.description: 4×8' au seuil (95-102 % FTP), récup 4' en Z1

coachingTipsEn: First minute at lower threshold, last minute at upper threshold
If the last rep drops more than 5 % power, the load was too high
Spin smooth, avoid mashing at the end of intervals
commonMistakesEn: Opening above threshold and blowing up on the third interval
Cutting recovery short to "go faster"

descriptionEn: Classic VO2max intervals. Five 3-minute blocks at 110-120 % FTP, 3 minutes recovery. Pushes maximal oxygen uptake.

mainSetTemplate.description: 5×3' en Z5 (110-120 % FTP), récup 3' en Z1

coachingTipsEn: Build power progressively over the first 45 seconds
High cadence (95-105 rpm) to reduce muscular load
Maximal breathing peaks around minute 2, that's expected
commonMistakesEn: Nuking the first interval and ruining the next four
Cutting the recovery short

Steady cadence 85-90 rpm on average, no lower on flat sections

Skipping fueling past 90 min

descriptionEn: Higher-volume sweet-spot variant. Three 12-minute blocks at 90-94 % FTP, 6 minutes recovery. Builds sustainable aerobic capacity without crossing into accumulating lactate fatigue.

warmupStructure.description: Échauffement progressif + 2×1' en Z3 pour activer

warmupTemplate.description: Échauffement progressif + 2×1' en Z3 pour activer

coachingTipsEn: If power drifts more than 5 % on the last block, the session is overcooked
Steady cadence around 90 rpm
Eat something between blocks if the session goes past 75 minutes

Cutting recovery short to finish earlier

descriptionEn: Neuromuscular activation. Eight all-out 30-second sprints (Z6+, ≥150 % FTP), 4 minutes full recovery. Improves peak power and motor unit recruitment without heavy cardiac load.

Start out of the saddle for maximum torque

Heart rate stays high between efforts, that's intentional
High cadence (95-105 rpm) to reduce muscular stress

If cadence rises above 80 rpm, shift up

Recovery = same duration as effort
Increasing intensity throughout the session
Created by Steve Moneghetti, Australian marathoner
commonMistakesEn: Starting too fast on the 90s
Not accelerating on the final 15s
Cutting recovery times

descriptionEn: Accessible fartlek for beginners. Eight short 30-second accelerations with generous recovery. Fun speed play.
coachingTipsEn: Accelerations are moderate, not sprints
Use visual landmarks (lampposts, trees)
The 90s recovery allows full recovery
Fun session to discover pace changes
commonMistakesEn: Sprinting from the first acceleration
Walking during recovery instead of jogging
Not having fun: fartlek is speed play

descriptionEn: Standard fartlek from Kenyan training camps. Strict alternation of 1 minute fast / 1 minute recovery for 30-40 minutes. Effort-based, no watch needed. Iconic Thursday session in Iten (Kenya).
coachingTipsEn: Effort is based on feel, not GPS pace, run by instinct like the Kenyans
Recovery is a sustained float jog, not walking or very slow jogging
Variation: use 2/1 or 3/1 ratios to vary the stimulus
commonMistakesEn: Running efforts too fast early and being unable to maintain over 20 reps
Recovering by walking instead of maintaining an active jog rhythm
Constantly checking the watch instead of feeling the effort

descriptionEn: Fartlek with progressively shorter but faster efforts. Pattern: 5min-4min-3min-2min-1min with 90-second recovery. Increasing intensity from tempo to sprint. Develops ability to accelerate in late race stages.
coachingTipsEn: Effort should increase progressively, don't sprint from the start
The last 1-minute effort should be the fastest of the entire session
90 seconds of recovery is enough to maintain flow without fully recovering
commonMistakesEn: Running the 5-minute effort too fast and being unable to accelerate later
Keeping the same pace on all efforts instead of progressively accelerating
Extending recoveries beyond 90 seconds

descriptionEn: Endurance-specific fartlek for half-marathon and marathon. Alternating 2 minutes at threshold pace / 1 minute jog for 40 minutes. High volume at moderate-high intensity. Classic Kenyan camp workout for marathon preparation.
coachingTipsEn: Threshold pace corresponds to your half-marathon pace or slightly faster
The recovery minute is a sustained jog, not walking
Key session for half-marathon and marathon: develops threshold endurance
commonMistakesEn: Running efforts too fast: this is threshold work, not VO2max
Recovering too slowly, which reduces the continuous aerobic stimulus
Not having enough endurance base to support 40 minutes of work

descriptionEn: Progressive fartlek with increasingly longer efforts: 1-2-3-4-5 minutes, with recovery equal to half the effort time. Teaches managing increasing effort and develops mental endurance. Ideal for marathon preparation.
coachingTipsEn: Effort should remain constant despite increasing duration, don't slow down on the 5min
Short recovery (half the effort time) maintains metabolic stress
Focus on your breathing: controlled during long efforts
commonMistakesEn: Starting too fast on the 1min and being unable to maintain subsequent efforts
Extending recoveries as efforts get longer
Mentally giving up on the 4 or 5 minutes, that's the core of the session

descriptionEn: Fartlek with random pace changes signaled by a whistle (or alarm). A partner or app decides when to change. Efforts from 15s to 3min, unpredictable. Simulates race pace changes.
